title: yami: sanitize values for coverity before tvb_get_string_enc used
description:
There were tainted scalar reported by coverity whuch needed to be sanitized.

`tainted_data: Passing tainted expression val_len to tvb_get_string_enc, which uses it as an allocation size.`

Use coverity annotation 3 times when `tvb_get_string_enc()` is used because within that function we eventually end up calling `ensure_contiguous_unsigned()` which will sanitizie its arguments anyway.

Coverity CID 1356246

AI-Assisted: no

notes.body:
@johnthacker, in Jan 2026 you added the coverity annotations to `tvb_ensure_bytes_exist()` if I see it correctly.

```
/* coverity[ +tainted_data_sanitize : arg-1 ] */
/* coverity[ +tainted_data_sanitize : arg-2 ] */
void
tvb_ensure_bytes_exist(const tvbuff_t *tvb, const unsigned offset, const int length)
```

However, when Coverity scans a file like `proto.c`, it doesn't necessarily have the implementation of `tvbuff.c` in its immediate memory. It only sees the declaration in `tvbuff.h`.

My understanding is:
- If the annotation is only in `tvbuff.c`: It only "washes" the data inside that specific file.
- If the annotation is in `tvbuff.h`: It tells Coverity: "Whenever anyone calls this function, assume the arguments passed to it are sanitized afterward."

If you check `proto.c` as an example, it still has CID 1680434 Untrusted allocation size even though it has `tvb_ensure_bytes_exist()`.

```
      	7. tainted_return_value: Function get_uint_value returns tainted data.[show details]
      	8. var_assign: Assigning: n = get_uint_value(tree, tvb, start, length, encoding), which taints n.
4280                n = get_uint_value(tree, tvb, start, length, encoding);
      	9. lower_bounds: Checking lower bounds of unsigned scalar n by taking the true branch of n > -1.
      	10. lower_bounds: Checking lower bounds of unsigned scalar n by taking the true branch of n > -1.
4281                tvb_ensure_bytes_exist(tvb, start + length, n);
4282                value = tvb_get_ptr(tvb, start + length, n);
      	
CID 1680434: (#2 of 2): Untrusted allocation size (TAINTED_SCALAR)
11. tainted_data: Passing tainted expression n to format_bytes_hfinfo, which uses it as an allocation size.
```

So what do you think about adding those 2 Coverity annotation lines to `tvbbuff.h` too?
Thanks, yes. I approved that other MR.

Since `tvb_get_string_enc()` (with ENC_ASCII) calls `ensure_contiguous_unsigned` (which is a static function in tvbuff.c), can you see if changing the annotation there to `+taint_sanitize` would resolve 1356246?

The second one would eliminate the Coverity warning, but the logic isn't exactly right. Each parameter is more than a byte (variable length, but at least 5 I believe), so there needs to be more than `count` bytes available. In practice, the taint is cleared because of adding all the items to the tree, which checks the length.

> I think coverity won't be able see 'inside' tvb_get_string_enc() to fix the tainted data. the coverity warning is that we pass a tainted variable to tvb_get_string_enc().

If so, that's a bug on Coverity's part. If you follow the CID on Coverity, it reports that a tainted value is passed to tvb_get_string_enc, which calls, say, `tvb_get_ascii_string`, which is annotated like so:

```c
            ptr = ensure_contiguous_unsigned(tvb, offset, length);
1. taint_sink_lv_call: Passing tainted expression length to taint sink get_ascii_string.[show details]
3287        return get_ascii_string(scope, ptr, length);
```

The `ensure_contiguous_unsigned()` call should sanitize `offset` and `length` at least for the following `get_ascii_string` call. If it doesn't, then we're presumably using the annotations incorrectly.

>  The only logical way to fix that is to sanitize the data before.

No, I think it is extremely **illogical** to do that, when the function itself already has a call to a sanitization function in it.

Please do not expect the Coverity engine to be that sophisticated to look forward into the next function to see if an argument or parameter would be sanitized later. 

Coverity only considers the return value of `tvb_get_letohl()` which is tainted and not handled (according to its logic). This is not a Coverity fault, this is how it's designed and works. It's not an AI engine.

> Please do not expect the Coverity engine to be that sophisticated to look forward into the next function to see if an argument or parameter would be sanitized later.

I am not saying that. I am saying that above if `ptr = ensure_contiguous_unsigned(tvb, offset, length);` sanitizes `offset` and `length`, then the *following* line, the function *after* `ensure_contiguous_unsigned`, the `get_ascii_string`, should know that those two are sanitized.

If that doesn't work, then calling `tvb_ensure_bytes_exist` in the outer calling function shouldn't work either.

Also, since the `tvb_ensure_bytes_exist` call is totally useless and inefficient, it would be better to add a Coverity annotation than call a unnecessary function - the unnecessary function should be commented anyway to indicate that it's only there to satisfy Coverity.

> Also, since the `tvb_ensure_bytes_exist` call is totally useless and inefficient, it would be better to add a Coverity annotation than call a unnecessary function - the unnecessary function should be commented anyway to indicate that it's only there to satisfy Coverity.

okay, so this means a design rule: avoid unnecessary function calls. Make sense.

The `tvb_get_letohl()` returns 4 bytes which means between 0 and UINT32_MAX so technically it is valid to check it against the remaining tvb length, so `tvb_ensure_bytes_exist()` is not completely unnecessary. However, there are plenty  other steps/functions in the code where we validate the length of remaining bytes so in a way we can say we do not need to validate it at that point of the code in this MR.

> I am not saying that. I am saying that above if `ptr = ensure_contiguous_unsigned(tvb, offset, length);` sanitizes `offset` and `length`, then the _following_ line, the function _after_ `ensure_contiguous_unsigned`, the `get_ascii_string`, should know that those two are sanitized.

Okay, now I understand what you were trying to say here. I believe I have an explanation to that but not sure how easy to prove it. It could be related to the forward declaration.

[Line 61](https://gitlab.com/wireshark/wireshark/-/blame/master/epan/tvbuff.c?ref_type=heads#L61): 
```
static inline const uint8_t*
ensure_contiguous_unsigned(tvbuff_t *tvb, const unsigned offset, const unsigned length);
```

So it may happen that our coverity annotations in line 935 becomes ineffective due to the forward declaration.
[Line 935](https://gitlab.com/wireshark/wireshark/-/blame/master/epan/tvbuff.c?ref_type=heads#L935): 
```
/* coverity[ +tainted_data_sanitize : arg-1 ] */
/* coverity[ +tainted_data_sanitize : arg-2 ] */
static inline const uint8_t*
ensure_contiguous_unsigned(tvbuff_t *tvb, const unsigned offset, const unsigned length)
```

To test it, I would add those coverity annotations in front of the forward declaration in line 61...

And also, this does not have the annotation correction either.

`tainted_data_sanitize` is deprecated, we need `taint_sanitize` similar to the updates in `tvbuff.h`.

I think it is a valid and good idea to add coverity annotations to `tvb_get_string_enc()` because it would help.

`tvbuff.h`:
```
/* coverity[ +taint_sanitize : arg-3 ] */
WS_DLL_PUBLIC uint8_t *tvb_get_string_enc(wmem_allocator_t *scope,
    tvbuff_t *tvb, const unsigned offset, const unsigned length, const unsigned encoding);

```

I have created a new MR to fix that annotation issue for `ensure_contiguous_unsigned` in `tvbuff.c` ...

!23857
@johnthacker any further comment, please?

Sure, we'll see if it works. We haven't had a great deal of success with Coverity comments, e.g. a0d4b464b6696e78ed4acb0df22e838ab49b07ef did not reduce the number of Coverity reports at all. This probably works here, but I assume there's some way to indicate via the function call to Coverity that the parameter is ok or else Coverity is a horribly broken tool. But it's probably us.

Most of the time, dissectors shouldn't have to worry about how big the tvb "buffer" is, they should be able to just call proto_tree_add_xxx and if the tvb is too small, exceptions are thrown (and execution of "unsanitized values" would be prevented).  The same would be true for proto_tree_add_xxx_ret_yyy.
With the additions here of tvb_ensure_bytes_exist() it limits the dissection of "short" packets (where count > tvb_remaining), but at least some of the parameters in the "count loop" could be dissectors before a bounds exception is thrown.
From looking at the dissector around the lines changed by this MR, I think the dissector just needs a little more of proto_tree_add_xxx_ret_yyy and hopefully that would quiet Coverity.

Indeed, the extra `tvb_ensure_bytes_exist` added here are pointless from a dissector logic and only to quiet Coverity, in which case they might as well be Coverity annotations.

Any time data is retrieved with byte swapping (which means Big Endian since we compile and submit to Coverity on Little Endian platforms), Coverity assumes that the data is tainted, which is fair.

If the data is a 16-bit unsigned quantity, and cast/stored in an int, Coverity will report that casting an unsigned value to a larger signed int effectively tests the lower bound as zero. For some reason it does *not* consider that this effectively tests the upper bound, even though the upper bound is bounded by 65535 by doing this.

We don't strongly care about loop bounds that are 16-bit values. We also don't strongly care about allocation sizes that are 16-bit either. (We could I suppose indicate that all 16-bit values are not actually tainted.)

If a 32-bit or larger value is used as a loop boundary, and the dissector does not call `proto_tree_add_xxx` with an offset that advances on each loop iteration, that is a problem (and that has caused errors with excessive time that turns into bugs reported by the fuzzers.)

If it does advance the offset every iteration and calls `proto_tree_add_xxx`, then if the number is too large, it will throw an exception and abort the loop. Coverity doesn't understand that, and I'm not sure how to make it understand that.

Similarly, using a value and calling `wmem_alloc()` on a buffer intending to copy into that buffer can be a untrusted allocation. The alternatives are to call `tvb_ensure_bytes_exist` or similar beforehand, or to call `tvb_memdup` which should sanitize the offset and length.

The original idea was to handle a false positive Coverity warning and not to impact the currently working WS code or logic. It is a good question where and how we might need to compromise: ignore the warning, use coverity annotations or minor code change to address the warning.

Every time a `tvb_get_letohl()` or similar called, Coverity will consider the return value tainted. I think it is accurate. Yes, same as John said: Any time data is retrieved with byte swapping (which means Big Endian since we compile and submit to Coverity on Little Endian platforms), Coverity assumes that the data is tainted, which is fair.

Yes, somehow the upper bound is the one not handled correctly and it is a good question why. But Coverity only looks at the return value of tvb_get_xxx and nothing more. It cannot "look ahead" into the next function to see if that function would sanitize the tainted data or not. I think that would be a very advanced tool do to such thing. Coverity is limited, do not expect to act as an AI engine to interpret the whole dissector.

The way forward, how I see:

1. **Ignore the warning**: yes, sure, we just keep it as it is. But there are thousands of false positive warnings so it is more difficult to find real issues which should be fixed.

2. **Coverity annotations**: starting to add in-line annotations is not a good idea and we would end up with way too many of those.

3. **Address the warning**: even though the code and logic do not require it, we can still fixe the warning if there is an intention to do so. Either we "do" what coverity missed and complains about, and we add an upper bound (`count < UINT32_MAX`) or we use a function such as `tvb_ensure_bytes_exist()` which is already used in other dissectors and since it has coverity annotations, it fixes the sanitization concerns.

I do not want to reinvent the wheel, I had only a minor intention to fix a false positive Coverity warning in an easy and simple way.

We have near 5,000 coverity warnings and it's very difficult to find the needle (real faults) in the haystack...

This MR was raised in good faith to address a minor issue with a minor fix.

So it the WS developers disagree with this change, it's ok, in that case just tell me to close the MR.

Thank you.

There are hundreds of existing false positives relating to `tvb_get_string_enc` (often via that function being possibly called by `proto_tree_add_item`). It would be great if we could figure out a way to handle them all via changes in tvbuff.c and possibly proto.c rather than in dissectors.
You need to add coverity annotations to those functions in the header files to sanitise certain arguments.

To be able clear those warnings, the tainted variable must be sanitized **before** it is used as a function's argument or the function has to have a **coverity annotation** to consider a particular attributed sanitized. Coverity's current implementation does not provide more options.

Also note, in an example below, it will still trigger Coverity alarm:

> Using tainted variable "count" as a loop boundary.

```
count = tvb_get_letohl(tvb, offset);
...
for (i = 0; i < count; i++) {
```

But the part I do not understand it that Coverity is incosistent. These TAINTED_SCALAR warnings are raised only for some dissectors/functions but it seems it's not raised for all occurrences.

For `packet-yami.c` there are only 3 warnings:
1. 1356246 Untrusted allocation size:
   [line 315](https://gitlab.com/wireshark/wireshark/-/blame/master/epan/dissectors/packet-yami.c?ref_type=heads#L315), tainted_data: Passing tainted expression val_len to tvb_get_string_enc, which uses it as an allocation size
2. 1356247 Untrusted loop bound:
   [line 407](https://gitlab.com/wireshark/wireshark/-/blame/master/epan/dissectors/packet-yami.c?ref_type=heads#L407), tainted_data: Using tainted variable count as a loop boundary.
3. 1680445 Resource leak:
   line 186, Variable repr going out of scope leaks the storage it points to.

But similar to item 2, the same code/logic is there multiple times in the dissector and no warning in Coverity.... for example  [line 285](https://gitlab.com/wireshark/wireshark/-/blame/master/epan/dissectors/packet-yami.c?ref_type=heads#L285), [line 307](https://gitlab.com/wireshark/wireshark/-/blame/master/epan/dissectors/packet-yami.c?ref_type=heads#L307), [line 367](https://gitlab.com/wireshark/wireshark/-/blame/master/epan/dissectors/packet-yami.c?ref_type=heads#L367) and so on...

To fix all `Using tainted variable count as a loop boundary` has a very simple way, the for loop needs a slight update:

`for (i = 0; i < count && count < UINT32_MAX; i++) {`

I know this is kind of ugly but I think this would be a very quick fix...

To address the Coverity issue `Using tainted variable count as a loop boundary`, the primary solution is to properly sanitize the input by checking its value against a permissible range. Coverity analysis is designed to recognize these validation checks automatically.

`count` is stored on 4 bytes which can be a huge number. You can create a "tainted" pcap where you identify the exact 4 bytes for `count` and change all 4 to 0xFF (or this can be a simple SW code mistake which sets the count to a huge value accidentally). Then the loop will run 4 billion times, potentially hanging the application or exhausting resources.

In Wireshark dissectors, ignoring this is risky, I believe. If `count` is huge, the loop will run until it hits the end of the packet, but even then, it might trigger a lot of "Expert Info" errors or malformed packet exceptions, which can make Wireshark crawl or crash.

To make the code more robust, we shall set an upper bound to `count`, and my earlier UINT32_MAX was not good enough, it should be much smaller than that...
@johnthacker, how would you like to proceed? Thank you.
